# Acts 9:1-22: Research notes

**Coverage:** Most of these notes come from verse-by-verse sources: Enduring Word (David Guzik), Precept Austin, Bible.org, and the older commentaries collected on Biblehub and Studylight. My copy of Guzik's page cut off around v. 10, so vv. 11–22 rest more on the other sources.

**Not found:** Nothing from bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes, oca.org, the Methodist sites (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage. Those are left out.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** This picks up from Acts 8:3, where Saul was already dragging believers off to prison. Now he widens the campaign to Damascus, about 130 miles (a six-day journey) from Jerusalem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- Guzik describes a violent man sure he was in the right. Saul was not looking for Jesus; Jesus came looking for him. Guzik names the high priest as Caiaphas. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- Precept Austin, citing A.T. Robertson: the Greek has the sense of breathing *in*. Threats and slaughter had become the very air Saul breathed. Barrett adds that "still" shows his hostility was ongoing and had not cooled. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-9-commentary
- Longenecker (via Precept Austin) suggests Saul may have justified himself by Old Testament examples of zeal against unfaithfulness, such as Phinehas (Numbers 25). https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-9-commentary

**v. 2:** "The Way" seems to be the earliest name for the Christian movement. It suggests that following Jesus is a way of living, not just a set of beliefs. The fact that Saul bothered with Damascus shows the church there was already sizeable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- Ironside makes the same point: Christianity is "a way." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/acts-9.html

**v. 3:** Guzik calls this unusual. God does not normally confront sinners with a light and a voice from heaven. Acts 22 and 26 add that it happened at midday and the light was brighter than the sun. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- Bible.org: the light was the light of Christ's glory. Saul "saw the light" and would himself become a light to the Gentiles. https://bible.org/seriespage/14-conversion-saul-acts-91-31
- Matthew Henry: Christ met him on the road, not in the temple or synagogue. Conversion is not tied to church settings. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_009.cfm
- Precept Austin sees irony here: on his way to arrest members of the Way, Saul was himself arrested by the One who is the Way. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-9-commentary

**v. 4:**
- **Falling down:** Guzik says Saul fell from sheer terror. None of the three accounts mentions a horse; that idea comes from paintings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- **"Saul, Saul":** Repeating a name shows deep feeling, not necessarily anger (compare "Martha, Martha"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- **Hebrew name:** Ellicott notes that only here and in v. 17 does the Greek use the Hebrew form of Saul's name. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-4.htm
- **"Why do you persecute Me?":** This is the most widely shared point across the sources. Persecuting the church is persecuting Christ, because the church is his body. Ligonier stresses that Jesus did not say "My church" but "Me." https://www.ligonier.org/posts/saul-saul-why-are-you-persecuting-me
- Biblehub's study notes say the sentence will later shape Paul's whole teaching on union with Christ. https://biblehub.com/acts/9-4.htm
- Matthew Henry: Saul had to see himself as a sinner before he could become a saint. Being humbled under conviction of sin is the first step in conversion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-4.html
- Constable, citing Longenecker: to a rabbi, a voice from heaven always meant a rebuke or instruction from God. Saul would have been baffled, since he thought he was *defending* God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-4.html

**v. 5:** Guzik: Saul knew exactly which Jesus was speaking, and may have heard him teach in Jerusalem. He also says the words about kicking against the goads, found in the KJV/NKJV here, were added by later copyists from Acts 22 and 26. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- Oswald Chambers (via Precept Austin): at the words "I am Jesus," Saul realised the one he persecuted was the Saviour, and he threw himself on his mercy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-9-commentary
- Ironside reads Saul's "Lord" as accepting Christ as Lord right there on the road. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/acts-9.html
- Don Stewart is more cautious. The Greek word can just mean "Sir," though most readers still take the moment as Saul's conversion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/baptism-with-the-holy-spirit/20-did-saul-receive-the-holy-spirit-after-his-conversion.cfm

**v. 6:** Jesus told him only the next step. Guzik says God often guides us one step at a time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- Precept Austin points out that the KJV words "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" appear only in the Textus Receptus. The lesson it draws is surrender: the redeemed respond with obedience. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-9-commentary
- Matthew Henry: Saul must wait, and first think over what he has already been told. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-9.html

**v. 7:** This verse is often compared with Acts 22:9 ("they did not hear/understand the voice"). Nearly all the older commentators harmonise the two: the men heard a sound but did not make out the words. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-7.html
- Barnes, Robertson, Bengel, Whedon and Scofield all take this line. https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-7.html
- Ellicott: they could not attach any meaning to the sounds that meant so much to Saul. https://biblehub.com/acts/9-7.htm
- A few older writers take a different route. Trapp and Poole think the men heard *Saul's* voice, not Christ's. https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-7.html
- Calvin openly admits that at first sight the two accounts do not seem to agree. https://pro.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-7.html

**v. 8:** Matthew Henry: the man who meant to lead Christians captive to Jerusalem was himself led captive to Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-9.html
- Guzik: he shut his eyes to God's light, so for a few days he was as blind in body as he had been in spirit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/

**v. 9:** Guzik: the three days were a humbling time of dying to self, before receiving resurrection life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- Constable rejects explaining the event away as hallucination, sunstroke or epilepsy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-9.html
- Ironside quotes Spurgeon's reply to the epilepsy theory: blessed epilepsy, if it produces a conversion like this. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/acts-9.html

**v. 10:** Ananias was an ordinary disciple, not an apostle or church officer. Guzik suggests this meant no one could say Paul got his gospel from a prominent man. God spoke to Ananias gently, and "Here I am, Lord" is the ideal reply. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/

**v. 11:**
- Straight Street can still be identified, running nearly a mile while the other streets are crooked. Naming the street and Judas's house is taken as evidence that the story is genuine. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/acts-9.html
- Barclay: it was a great street running east to west across Damascus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/acts-9.html

**vv. 13–14:** Ananias was afraid because he knew what Saul had done in Jerusalem and planned to do in Damascus. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-9-commentary
- Matthew Henry: the believers in Damascus trembled like lambs before a wolf. Saul's conversion was their protection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-9.html

**vv. 15–16:** Precept Austin links Jesus' words to Ananias with Saul's commission to carry Christ's name to Gentiles, kings and Israel. The enemy of Jesus became his devoted apostle. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-9-commentary

**v. 17:**
- **"Brother Saul":** Barnes says this recognises him as a fellow Christian. Laying on hands was not ordination but the usual way of passing on a blessing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-17.htm
- **Confirmation for Saul:** Ananias knew about the road encounter, which he could only have learned from Jesus. Precept Austin says this would have strengthened Saul's faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-9-commentary

**v. 18:** Luke uses a Greek medical term for the "scales." The cure was instant, which shows it was a miracle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-18.htm
- Barnes: like other early converts, Saul was baptized immediately. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-18.htm
- Clarke: baptism was Saul's public profession of faith and proved he was sincere. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-18.html

**v. 19:** Guzik: God cared for Saul's physical needs as well as his spiritual ones. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Act/Act_9.cfm
- Bible.org: the first proof of his conversion was that he joined the church. The man who wanted to kill the saints now wanted their company. https://bible.org/seriespage/14-conversion-saul-acts-91-31

**v. 20:**
- Ironside: Peter had preached Jesus as the Servant; Saul now preached him as the Son of God. Ironside also places Paul's trip to Arabia (Galatians 1:17) within this period. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/acts-9.html
- Barclay recommends reading this alongside Galatians 1:15–24 to get the order of events. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/acts-9.html

**v. 21:** Everyone noticed the change. People remembered both his reputation and why he had come to Damascus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/acts-9.html

**v. 22:**
- Matthew Henry says the Greek word for "proving" means affirming and confirming, teaching so as to persuade. He thinks Saul helped build up the very church he came to destroy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_009.cfm
- Precept Austin estimates about 20,000 Jews lived in Damascus. They were dismayed both by Saul's reversal and by his preaching. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-9-commentary

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**When was Saul saved? (vv. 5–9, 17–18)**
- **Saved on the road:** This is the common evangelical view. Stewart says most Bible students take it this way. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/baptism-with-the-holy-spirit/20-did-saul-receive-the-holy-spirit-after-his-conversion.cfm
- Constable: Paul was born again on the road, and was baptized after calling on the Lord. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/22-16.html
- **Saved in Damascus:** Guzik quotes Lenski, who says the conversion began on the road but was not completed until faith came in Damascus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- **Uncertain:** Bible.org says we don't know exactly when, though it seems not to have been on the road. https://bible.org/seriespage/14-conversion-saul-acts-91-31

**What baptism does (v. 18, with Acts 22:16)**
- **Baptism as a symbol:** GotQuestions says Paul believed before Ananias came and received the Spirit before baptism. So "wash away your sins" must describe what baptism symbolises. https://www.gotquestions.org/baptism-Acts-22-16.html
- Precept Austin agrees: the baptism did not pass on the Spirit or forgiveness, and Paul was not a sacramentalist. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-19-commentary
- **Immersion:** Gill (Baptist) argues that "arose and was baptized" shows immersion. If water had been poured or sprinkled, Saul could have stayed seated. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-18.html
- **Reformed:** Calvin says Paul's sins were already forgiven. Baptism did not wash him alone; it gave fresh confirmation of grace he already had. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/22-16.html
- **Lutheran:** Sam Schuldheisz (1517.org) reads the story as a death and resurrection, and says "Baptism is your Damascus road." In baptism Jesus does for us what he did for Saul, and the scales of unbelief fall from our hearts. https://www.1517.org/articles/baptism-is-your-damascus-road
- **Baptism for forgiveness:** Some commentators on Studylight and CCEL argue that Saul was still in his sins until he was baptized. They point to the lack of rejoicing in v. 9 and to Acts 22:16. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/acts-9.html and https://ccel.org/contrib/exec_outlines/cia/cia_05.htm

**"Filled with the Holy Spirit" (v. 17)**
- **Pentecostal:** The Assemblies of God says Paul was converted on the road but not filled with the Spirit until three days later. Like the Samaritans in Acts 8, this shows a person can be a Christian without yet being filled. https://news.ag.org/en/articles/spiritual-life/2024/05/i-believe-in-the-baptism-in-the-holy-spirit
- **Against a "second blessing":** Don Stewart says v. 17 speaks of being *filled* (controlled by the Spirit), not *baptized*, in the Spirit. He sees no evidence here of a second work of grace. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/baptism-with-the-holy-spirit/20-did-saul-receive-the-holy-spirit-after-his-conversion.cfm
- **A middle view (John Piper):** Piper links being filled in v. 17 with the extraordinary power that confounded the Jews in v. 22. In Luke, being filled is for power in ministry. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/you-will-be-baptized-with-the-holy-spirit
- Piper also says Luke treats receiving the Spirit as a real experience, whether it happens in one step, two steps, or repeated fillings. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/what-does-it-mean-to-receive-the-holy-spirit
- **Older commentators:**
  - One older commentary on Biblehub (unnamed in what I read) suggests the gift was probably shown by speaking in tongues and prophetic insight. It also notes that Ananias was not an apostle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-17.htm
  - Another older note on the same page says Saul received the Spirit *before* baptism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-17.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary, by contrast, assumes the Spirit came only after baptism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-17.htm
  - Coffman argues from v. 18 that the Spirit followed baptism. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-18.html

---

## 3. Other views

**Catholic and Orthodox:**
- On v. 4, Augustine says Christ is head and body together, which is why he could say "why do you persecute Me." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701028.htm
- Augustine also notes that the Head cried out for its members, yet said "Me," not "My members." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801040.htm
- On v. 7, Catholic Answers reads the two accounts as saying the men heard the sound but did not understand the words. It compares John 12:28–29 and concludes there is no contradiction. https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/pauls-conversion
- I found no Orthodox (oca.org) source.

**Modern scholarship:**
- I found no Bibleodyssey or NET Bible notes on this passage.
- The only critical point I came across is the one Guzik reports: most scholars say the "goads" wording in vv. 5–6 was added by later copyists. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- Constable and Ironside mention sceptical explanations (hallucination, sunstroke, epilepsy) only in order to reject them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-9.html

**Popular modern teaching (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** I found nothing on this passage from these movements.
